questions.prompt: What is the most common way scientists share the results of an experiment?
questions.explain: A lab report explains what was done and found, so others can read it and learn from it.

questions.prompt: What does the title of a lab report tell the reader?
questions.explain: The title is a short label that tells readers the topic right away.

questions.prompt: Which part of a lab report lists the equipment needed?
questions.explain: The materials section lists everything you need, and can include a sketch of the setup.

questions.prompt: What does accuracy mean for a measurement?
questions.answer: How close it is to the true value
questions.explain: An accurate measurement is close to the real, correct value.

questions.prompt: What does precision mean for measurements?
questions.answer: How consistent and exact they are
questions.explain: Precise measurements are exact and come out nearly the same each time you repeat them.

questions.prompt: What is an estimation?
questions.answer: A rough guess based on reasoning and observing
wrong: An answer copied from a friend
questions.explain: When an exact measurement isn't possible, scientists use reasoning to make a close guess.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a scientist to be unbiased?
questions.answer: Having no special interest in the outcome
wrong: Being paid to get a certain answer
questions.explain: An unbiased scientist doesn't gain anything from one result over another, so the test stays fair.

questions.prompt: Why is it important for scientists to share their results?
questions.answer: So others can check and build on the work
wrong: So nobody else needs to do science
So they can keep their methods secret
So their results can never change
questions.explain: Sharing lets other scientists review, repeat and add to the work. That's how science grows.

questions.prompt: Which part of a lab report states the question you are trying to answer?
questions.explain: The purpose explains why you did the experiment and what question it tries to answer.

questions.prompt: Which of these belongs in the conclusion of a lab report?
questions.answer: Whether the results supported the hypothesis
wrong: A list of the beakers used
questions.explain: A conclusion sums up what you learned, any errors, and new questions to explore.

questions.prompt: How should data be shown in a lab report?
questions.answer: Organized in tables, graphs or drawings
questions.explain: Organized data with labels and titles is much easier for readers to understand.

questions.prompt: When should you write down your observations?
wrong: Only if they match your hypothesis
questions.explain: It's easy to forget details, so recording right away keeps your data accurate.

questions.prompt: Round 4.37 to the nearest tenth.
questions.explain: Look at the hundredths digit. It is 7, which is 5 or more, so the tenths digit rounds up to 4.4.

questions.prompt: A rock's true mass is 50 g. You measure it three times and get 42 g, 42 g and 42 g. These measurements are...
questions.explain: They all match each other (precise), but they are far from the true 50 g (not accurate).

questions.prompt: A pencil is truly 10.0 cm long. Which set of measurements is both accurate and precise?
questions.explain: These are close to each other and close to the true length. The 8 cm set is precise but not accurate.

questions.prompt: Round 6.25 to the nearest tenth.
questions.explain: The hundredths digit is 5. When it is 5 or more, you round up, so 6.25 becomes 6.3.

questions.prompt: A candy company pays for a study that finds its candy is healthy. Why should you be careful about the result?
questions.answer: The company may be biased toward a good result
wrong: Candy can't be studied by science
The study used too many people
questions.explain: The company gains money if the result looks good, so it has a special interest in the outcome.

questions.prompt: Which question best helps you judge another scientist's results?
questions.answer: Can other people repeat the results?
wrong: Does the graph use many colors?
questions.explain: Results that others can repeat are much more trustworthy than results that only happened once.

questions.prompt: When would a scientist most likely estimate instead of measuring exactly?
questions.answer: When the right tool isn't available
wrong: When they have a perfect ruler
When the object is easy to measure
When they want a random answer
questions.explain: Estimation is useful when an exact measurement isn't possible or practical.

questions.prompt: Kids who eat breakfast get better grades in a study. What is a good scientific question to ask about this?
questions.answer: Could something else explain the better grades?
wrong: How can we hide this result?
questions.explain: Good scientists check whether the data could be explained another way before trusting a conclusion.
